headline: Marsh Grass Turning Gold, Bunker Pushing In — Blues Rule the River Mouth
subhead: The shad run is a distant memory, but peanut bunker pouring off Great Island have turned the mouth into a bluefish highway while the stripers wait on cooler nights.
body_markdown:
Walk the breakwater at Saybrook Point this week and you'll see it before you feel it — the marsh grass out toward Great Island has gone from green to that first dusty gold, and the ospreys that spent June and July hauling menhaden up to the nest platforms are mostly gone, fledged and off south already. That's the calendar telling you what the thermometer hasn't quite caught up to yet. The river's still carrying summer warmth on the surface, but the nights are cooling, and every guide who's run this stretch for a few decades knows what that combination means: bunker start balling up in the coves, and the blues find them before the stripers commit to anything serious.

That's exactly the pattern right now. Peanut bunker have flooded into the lower river — thick pods stacking along the edges off Great Island, working in and out of Calves Island and down toward the outer bar on the tide — and bluefish have taken that as an invitation. Boats working the mouth on the last two hours of the ebb have been finding blues busting bunker on top, sometimes visible from the Point itself, slashing through pods that get pinned against the current seam where the river dumps into the Sound. That's a sight worth chasing with a bucktail or a Kastmaster — 2 to 3-ounce, white or chartreuse, cast into the commotion and worked with a fast, erratic retrieve. No finesse needed. These blues, 3 to 6 pounds mostly with some better fish mixed in, are eating with intent, and a popper thrown right into a boil off the Saybrook breakwater or the flats below Great Island will get hit as fast as you can crank it.

Stripers are in the mix, but they're playing a different game than the blues right now, and that's worth being honest about. The bass are mostly holding under the bunker schools rather than crashing them on top, picking off cripples and stragglers on the drop rather than committing to a full blitz. That means the better program for bass has been working soft plastics and swimming plugs down through the water column rather than fishing the surface show. A white Al's Goldfish or a 5-inch white/pearl soft plastic swimbait, fished on the last two hours of the ebb along the channel edge off North Cove and down past Calves Island toward the mouth, has been picking up schoolies and some slot-class fish holding tight to the drop-off where the river current meets the harder Sound water. Depth's been in the 8 to 15-foot range along those edges, and the take is subtle — a soft pull rather than a slam — which tells you these fish aren't in a hurry yet.

White perch fishing has quietly been solid for anyone willing to slow down and fish deep. The holes below the Baldwin Bridge and up into the Essex reaches have been holding good numbers, and small bucktail jigs tipped with a piece of bloodworm or a sliver of shrimp, worked slow along bottom in 15 to 20 feet, have been steady producers on the last of the incoming. It's not glamorous fishing, but it's dependable, and it's a good option on the days when the wind kicks up out on the flats and makes the bunker chase uncomfortable.

We flagged last week that conditions in this stretch would hold stable through the near term, and that's exactly what's played out — no big shift in water temperature, no major push of new bait, just the same warm-water pattern grinding along with the bluefish carrying the show. That's typical for this river. It tends to lag the open Sound by a week or two on anything seasonal, whether that's the spring shad run coming in behind the rest of the coast or the fall transition arriving late. Out west in the Sound, the water's sitting in the low 70s and blues have been the most dependable predator around bait schools for weeks now — the same story that's playing out here at the mouth, just with a river current mixed in instead of open water.

Looking at the next several days, don't expect a wholesale changeover yet. The moon's building toward full, which should tighten up the tide and start concentrating bait more aggressively in the usual pinch points — the bar off Great Island, the seam below the breakwater, the mouth of North Cove. That's typically the first real trigger for stripers to shift from picking at scraps to committing harder, and if the pattern holds the way it usually does this time of year, look for that shift to show up in the next one to two weeks rather than this weekend. For now, the smart play is fishing the bluefish blitzes when they show — they're reliable and they're fun — while working the plugs and soft plastics underneath for the bass that are still playing it patient. If the wind stays manageable out of the south and southwest, early morning and the last two hours of the ebb remain the windows worth building a trip around, whether that's off the Point, down along Great Island, or working the deeper bends up toward Essex for perch when the top-water action goes quiet.
